title: DSA in Java: linked lists, trees and heaps
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.
description: Java versions of linked list, tree and heap problems: iterative reversal, level order with a Queue, LCA, PriorityQueue comparators and top-k, and an LRU cache on LinkedHashMap.
source: Oracle Java documentation (PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque, LinkedHashMap, Comparator); LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview

questions.prompt: Write a Java method ListNode reverse(ListNode head) that reverses a singly linked list iteratively (ListNode has int val and ListNode next) and returns the new head.

checks.label: loops while the current node is not null
saves the next node before rewiring
points the current node back to the previous one
returns the previous pointer as the new head

questions.explanation: Save next first, or you lose the rest of the list. The loop runs n times with O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) returning the values level by level, using a Queue (TreeNode has int val, TreeNode left and right).

checks.label: uses a Queue backed by ArrayDeque or LinkedList
processes one level at a time using the queue size
dequeues with poll or remove
enqueues the left and right children when present
returns the result list

questions.explanation: Capture q.size() before the inner loop: it is the number of nodes on the current level. Guard the null root, because ArrayDeque.offer(null) throws.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method TreeNode lca(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) returning the lowest common ancestor of nodes p and q in a binary tree (both exist; compare nodes with ==).
questions.starter:
static TreeNode lca(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
  
}

checks.label: returns root on null or when root is p or q
recurses into the left subtree
recurses into the right subtree
returns root when both sides found something

questions.explanation: If p and q are found in different subtrees the current node is their meeting point; if only one side finds anything, bubble that result up. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method List<Integer> topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) that returns the k most frequent values, counting with a HashMap and keeping a min-heap (PriorityQueue) of at most k entries.
questions.starter:
static List<Integer> topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
  
}

checks.label: counts frequencies in a map
creates a PriorityQueue ordered by the count
evicts the smallest count once the heap exceeds k
offers entries to the heap
returns the selected values

questions.explanation: A size-k min-heap keeps the k best seen so far and evicts the weakest, giving O(n log k). Bucket sort by frequency is O(n) and is an accepted alternative.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class LRUCache<K, V> that extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> and evicts the least recently used entry once the size exceeds a given capacity.
questions.starter:
class LRUCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
  
}

checks.label: stores the capacity from the constructor
calls super with accessOrder = true
overrides removeEldestEntry
evicts when size() exceeds the capacity

questions.explanation: accessOrder = true makes every get move the entry to the end, and removeEldestEntry is called after each put. In an interview you may also be asked to build the hash map plus doubly linked list by hand.

questions.prompt: A min-heap PriorityQueue<Integer> receives offers of 9, 4, 7, 1, 6, 2 in that order, then poll() is called twice. What does peek() return?
questions.explanation: The first two polls remove 1 and 2, the two smallest values. The remaining values are 4, 6, 7 and 9, so the head is 4.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Merging K sorted lists with N total nodes using a PriorityQueue of list heads costs O(N log K).
questions.reason: The PriorityQueue can grow to hold all N nodes at the same time.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true and the queue holds at most K entries (one head per list), so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each of the N nodes is offered and polled once at O(log K). Divide and conquer (merge pairs of lists) gives the same bound with O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Constructing a PriorityQueue from an existing collection of n elements takes O(n) time, faster than offering the elements one by one.
questions.reason: Half of the nodes of a binary heap are leaves, and the bulk build sifts down only from the internal nodes.

whys.a: Correct: most nodes sit near the bottom and travel only a short distance, so the sum of work is linear.
whys.b: R is the reason for the linear bound, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Bulk heapify is O(n); n separate offers are O(n log n). The same holds for any binary heap implementation.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.

whys.a: R has nothing to do with the cost of reading the head.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but thread safety does not explain the constant-time read; the head is simply the array element at index 0.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: peek is O(1), offer and poll are O(log n), and contains or remove(Object) are O(n). Use PriorityBlockingQueue when you need thread safety.

questions.prompt: Match each PriorityQueue call with its behaviour.

right.text: Reads the head without removing it, returning null when empty
Removes and returns the head, returning null when empty
Reads the head and throws NoSuchElementException when empty
Removes one matching element, scanning the queue in O(n)
Inserts x and sifts it up in O(log n)
Returns every element in sorted order in O(n)

questions.explanation: Know which methods throw and which return null, and that removing an arbitrary element is linear. That is why Dijkstra solutions use lazy deletion.

questions.prompt: In Java you need a max-heap of int values that may include Integer.MIN_VALUE. Which PriorityQueue construction is safe?

options.why: Correct: reverseOrder compares with compareTo and cannot overflow.

options.text: new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b - a) using plain subtraction
options.why: Subtraction can overflow for values far apart, such as Integer.MIN_VALUE, and give the wrong sign.

options.text: new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a - b) and read from the tail
options.why: This is a min-heap, and the tail of the backing array is not the maximum.

options.text: new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.max()) with a null comparator
options.why: Collections.max is not a Comparator, and a null comparator gives natural (min) ordering.

questions.explanation: Prefer Integer.compare(b, a) or Comparator.reverseOrder() over subtraction. Subtracting comparators are a classic latent overflow bug.

questions.prompt: A Java validator isValid(node, int lo, int hi) is first called with Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE and requires lo < node.val < hi. Which valid BST does it wrongly reject?

options.text: A tree with duplicate values on the left side
options.why: Duplicates are normally invalid in a BST, so rejecting them is the expected behaviour.

options.text: A tree that is a straight chain of left children
options.why: The bounds shrink correctly down a chain, so valid chains pass.

options.text: A perfectly balanced tree with seven nodes
options.why: Balanced trees pass; only extreme values at the sentinels break the check.

options.text: A single node whose value is Integer.MAX_VALUE
options.why: Correct: the strict check MAX_VALUE < MAX_VALUE fails even though the tree is valid.

questions.explanation: Use Long bounds, or null bounds for "no limit". Checking only the parent (not the ancestors' bounds) is the other classic validate-BST bug.

questions.text: To keep the k largest numbers, hold a {1}-heap of size {2}; after each offer, if the size exceeds k call {3} to drop the smallest.
questions.explanation: The root of that min-heap is the k-th largest so far, so a new value only matters if it beats the root.

questions.prompt: Iterating over or printing a Java PriorityQueue returns its elements in sorted order.

options.why: Only the head is guaranteed to be the smallest.
Correct: the backing array is only heap-ordered. Offering 5, 3, 8, 1 prints [1, 3, 8, 5].

questions.explanation: Poll repeatedly (or copy and sort) if you need sorted output. I ran the 5, 3, 8, 1 example and got [1, 3, 8, 5].

questions.prompt: In a Java PriorityQueue, contains(x) and remove(x) take O(n) time because the queue has to scan the array.

options.why: Correct: the heap ordering gives no way to find an arbitrary value without scanning.
It is linear: only the head is cheap to reach.

questions.explanation: If you need fast arbitrary removal, use a TreeSet or a TreeMap, or use lazy deletion.
